title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 8
paragraphs: This Candaules had fallen passionately in love with his own wife, and being in love, he came to believe that she was far more beautiful than any other woman. With this conviction, he began to confide in Gyges, the son of Dascylus — for Gyges was his favorite among the royal guards — speaking to him of the most important matters of state, and above all praising his wife's beauty beyond measure. And after no great time, since misfortune was destined to befall Candaules, he spoke to Gyges as follows: “Gyges, I don't think you believe me when I describe my wife's beauty — people's ears are less trusting than their eyes. So you must find some way to see her naked.” Gyges cried out and said, “Master, what an unwise thing to say! You are telling me to look upon my mistress naked? When a woman takes off her tunic, she takes off her modesty with it. There are fine old sayings handed down from long ago by which we should learn wisdom — and among them is this: let each man look upon his own. I do indeed believe that she is the most beautiful of all women, and I beg you not to ask of me what I am not permitted to do.”
